evidence_set: The highlights say immunoassays have many weaknesses that can result in false-positive and false-negative results, and that testing for designer drugs (for example synthetic cathinones and cannabinoids) is challenging because the compounds keep changing and new ones keep appearing. Screens are immunoassays, run in a laboratory or on site as point-of-care tests, which in general use antibodies to detect drug metabolites or classes of drug metabolites; point-of-care tests have the same limitations as laboratory immunoassays and should be used only to screen. All initial immunoassay results are presumptive; GC-MS, considered the criterion standard for confirmation, can identify specific molecular structures and quantifies what is present, but it is time-consuming and costly and is therefore reserved for confirming positive screens; LC-MS/MS is an alternative.

Table 4, adapted from an earlier review in the same journal by three of the four authors (reference 12: Moeller, Lee and Kissack, 2008), lists by screen the medicines that may not be detected, with no tests, concentrations or frequencies: benzodiazepine screens, alprazolam, clonazepam and lorazepam; cannabinoid screens, nabilone and synthetic cannabinoids; opioid, opiate and heroin screens, buprenorphine, fentanyl, meperidine, methadone, oxycodone and oxymorphone (p. 6) and tramadol (p. 7); 'not applicable' for the alcohol, amphetamine, cocaine, phencyclidine, tricyclic antidepressant and synthetic cannabinoid screens. The same table lists opiates (codeine, hydromorphone, hydrocodone, morphine) among the potential positives on opioid screens. Footnote b: newer immunoassays have corrected the false-positive amphetamine result from the Vicks inhaler.

Urine drug tests may not detect all opioids equally. Most conventional opiate immunoassays use morphine as the single calibrator that sets the line between a positive and a negative result; because the antibodies cross-react little with other opiates such as oxycodone, hydrocodone, hydromorphone and oxymorphone, there may be a risk of false negatives, and more advanced immunoassays or LC-MS/MS show higher specificity and can maximize detection of these. Fentanyl, methadone and buprenorphine differ in chemical structure from morphine, so commonly marketed morphine-specific immunoassays do not react to them; they require immunoassays specific for these compounds or LC-MS/MS. Some laboratories do not routinely test for semisynthetic or synthetic opioids in a standard opioid test unless specially requested, and clinicians are told to know their laboratory's immunoassays and its access to LC-MS/MS before testing. GC-MS, LC-MS/MS and other procedures to measure tramadol and its metabolites in urine have been developed (p. 11).

Interpreting benzodiazepine immunoassays can be complex, partly because they cannot tell individual benzodiazepines apart. Two significant limitations may lead to false negatives: the immunoassays cannot detect conjugated metabolites, and the cutoffs are high. Most are designed to detect the free (unconjugated) forms of oxazepam or nordiazepam, metabolites shared by several benzodiazepines (for example diazepam, chlordiazepoxide and temazepam); many benzodiazepines, for example lorazepam and alprazolam, are excreted as glucuronide conjugates and are not detected by most immunoassays unless the urine is first hydrolysed with beta-glucuronidase, which most laboratories do not do. Clonazepam, reduced mainly to 7-aminoclonazepam and not converted to oxazepam, may give a false negative and does not cross-react well. Cutoffs of 200 or 300 ng/mL were first set on the basis of older benzodiazepines such as diazepam, oxazepam and flurazepam and are often too high for lorazepam, alprazolam and triazolam; Fraser and Meatherall found that lowering the cutoff for alprazolam and triazolam to 100 ng/mL, with enzyme hydrolysis, increased positive results, and West et al. recommended 40 ng/mL to detect 7-aminoclonazepam.

More than 15 benzodiazepines are commercially available in the United States and large numbers of others in other countries (1st paragraph). The 6th paragraph sets the high rate of false-negative results on benzodiazepine immunoassays against the few medications that produce false-positive results on them (Table 4); it gives no figure for false negatives (its only rates are for false positives with sertraline, 27% to 32% in 2 retrospective studies).

Nabilone, a prescribed synthetic cannabinoid, tests negative for THC because of its distinct metabolites (p. 7). Synthetic cannabinoids are not detected as cannabis on urine drug tests (p. 15). Several immunoassays and point-of-care tests have been made for synthetic cannabinoids, but new compounds keep being developed, which makes testing for specific ones in urine difficult; little or no parent drug reaches urine; most assays are designed to detect metabolites of JWH-018 and JWH-073, with broader detection because many synthetic cannabinoids share the same structural pathway (the review's words), and because most have similar metabolic pathways the compound taken is hard to identify (pp. 15-16). No cutoff has been standardized: there is no acceptable cutoff value, and assays may range from 5 to 25 ng/mL. In Barnes et al., an ELISA kit for JWH-018 metabolites was tested against 73 synthetic cannabinoids: metabolites of several others cross-reacted significantly; raising the cutoff from 5 to 10 µg/L increased false-negative results by 12% (of what is not stated); and the test was limited in detecting newer compounds such as PB-22, RCS-4, RCS-8, XRL-11 and AKB48 (p. 16).

Single-author review published under the heading 'Basel Proceedings', by an author from the Clinical Biology Laboratory of Ghent University Hospital, with no stated search, selection criteria or appraisal. The Conclusion says the chances of detecting a substance increase if the most sensitive methods are used (tandem mass spectrometry, negative chemical ionization), if the metabolite that persists longest is chosen, and if the body fluid that allows the longest detection time is available (p. 204).
